articles_and_episodes.summary: by Rodney Hide The Post ran two pieces on the election a day apart. Big money, dark money and engineered overhangs, he says, may have swung the result. The government won not on argument but on cash and “cynically distorting the process”. articles_and_episodes.title: Labour’s route to power is all uphill
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Rodney Hide Last week I wrote that I couldn’t see what Labour could do about 2029. So I had the numbers run. Start with the board. Say National again wins 42 electorates, and that more National voters split their vote, say another 225,000. ACT and NZ First then take 15% of the party vote each, assuming an even split. On that model, the House grows to 142 seats. National’s overhang jumps from seven to 18. The right has 78 seats. It needs 72. That is a majority of six, not one. That is Labour’s hole. There are four ways out. Route one: win the voters back. Persuade right voters to vote Labour or Green. The trouble is how much it takes. While National holds its 42 electorates, every point Labour wins off the right mostly comes out of ACT and NZ First list seats. National’s seats don’t move. Its overhang just grows, and the House gets bigger. On the model, Labour, the Greens and the Maori Party, with Opportunity, need a swing of about seven points from the right to get a majority. articles_and_episodes.title: KIRRALIE SMITH: Binary Australia Director: ‘Who Decides?’ Documentary Challenges Australia’s Gender Policies
Shifting positions
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Rodney Hide David Farrar spent the campaign fighting the overhang. He is National’s pollster. He wrote against it. He warned against it at around 40 to 50 public talks. He went on Reality Check Radio, which was campaigning for it, to make the case against it. On Friday, on Kiwiblog, he went back through those arguments. Most of them, he now says, no longer apply. People, he writes, have not fully realised how much the 2026 result will shape 2029. He had five. National would have no list MPs. It would lose its best candidates, and could not recruit through the list. A government formed by a deliberate overhang would face a public backlash. Every party would then try to manipulate the system. And it would treat National, ACT and NZ First as interchangeable. Four of those, he admits, have already happened, or no longer hurt National. The party has no list MPs left. Anyone expecting to be a National list MP in 2029, he says, should buy a Lotto ticket. National now is an electorate-only party.
